proof:
# Sampled peak, coarse volume, and a one-coordinate depth budget

This note proves a sharp inequality involving the largest ACTUALLY
SAMPLED fiber, rather than the largest fiber over a real base. It
requires neither a dense grid nor equality of the body with the hull
of its sampled points. Its depth consequence uses the ordinary
continuous Grunbaum theorem on one actual fine fiber, with an explicit
coarse-volume hypothesis. No unrestricted OC conclusion is asserted.

## 1. Sharp sampled-peak bound

Let s>=1, h>0, and let Q be a compact convex set in R_u times R^s_x.
Sample the base on a+hZ. Let P be the finite set of sampled bases
having a NONEMPTY fiber. Write

    w_j=vol_s(Q_j),       T=sum_(j in P) w_j,
    W=max_(j in P) w_j,   A=vol_(s+1)(Q),

with T=W=0 when P is empty. Then

    A >= h(T-W).                                         (1)

Nonempty fibers of zero s-volume remain in P. If P has at most one
point, or T=0, (1) follows immediately from A>=0. Otherwise enumerate
P consecutively as u_0,...,u_(N-1), with u_(j+1)-u_j=h. They are
consecutive because the real projection of a convex set is an interval.

Brunn--Minkowski and the actual fiber inclusion give, for 0<=t<=1,

    vol_s(Q_((1-t)u_j+t u_(j+1)))
       >= [(1-t) w_j^(1/s)+t w_(j+1)^(1/s)]^s
       >= min(w_j,w_(j+1)).                              (2)

The sampled roots w_j^(1/s) form a nonnegative concave sequence.
Consequently the weights themselves are unimodal, allowing a flat
plateau at their maximum. For EVERY nonnegative unimodal finite
sequence,

    sum_(j=0)^(N-2) min(w_j,w_(j+1))=T-W.                (3)

To check (3), choose any index attaining W: before that index the
minimum is the left term, and after it the minimum is the right
term. The sum includes every weight except that one maximum.
Integrating (2) over the N-1 disjoint grid intervals and ignoring
any additional nonnegative volume outside them proves (1).

The unsampled maximum can be arbitrarily larger than W. This does
not enter the argument: the interpolant is used only as a LOWER
bound for the actual fiber-volume function.

## 2. Exact interpolation and a quantitative variation term

The proof actually gives the sharper exact expression

    A >= h sum_(j=0)^(N-2) Phi_s(w_j^(1/s),w_(j+1)^(1/s)), (4)

where

    Phi_s(a,b)=integral_0^1 [(1-t)a+tb]^s dt
              =[sum_(k=0)^s a^k b^(s-k)]/(s+1).          (5)

This polynomial formula includes a=b and zero endpoints. If a>=b,
each mixed monomial a^k b^(s-k), 1<=k<=s-1, is at least b^s.
Hence

    Phi_s(a,b)>=min(a^s,b^s)+|a^s-b^s|/(s+1).

Defining TV(w)=sum_(j=0)^(N-2)|w_(j+1)-w_j| gives

    A >= h[T-W+TV(w)/(s+1)].                             (6)

For a nonempty unimodal sequence, TV(w)=2W-w_0-w_(N-1).
Thus, when N>=1, the equivalent endpoint formula is

    A/h >= T-[(s-1)/(s+1)]W-[w_0+w_(N-1)]/(s+1).        (7)

For N=1, set TV=0; formulas (6)--(7) reduce to A>=0. For an
empty sampled set, (4) and (6) use empty sums and TV=0; (7) is
not asserted because it has no endpoint weights. The
coefficient 1/(s+1) in (6) is sharp: take the convex hull of an
s-dimensional body K at u=0 and a point at u=h. Then T=W=|K|,
TV=W, and A=hW/(s+1), by direct cone integration.

For s=1, (7) is the usual trapezoidal lower bound. For every s it
applies to an arbitrary convex Q, even with unsampled boundary
pieces. The root interpolant in (4) is exact for appropriately
homothetic affine-root fibers, but no homothety is assumed in the
inequalities.

## 3. Complete equality statement for (1)

Suppose T>0 and N>=2. Equality in (1) holds IF AND ONLY IF there
are an s-dimensional convex body K and a vector v in R^s such that

    Q={(u,x): u_0<=u<=u_(N-1),
                x in K+[(u-u_0)/(u_(N-1)-u_0)]v}.       (8)

Thus the base endpoints are grid points and Q is an affine shear
of a constant-volume product. In particular all sampled weights
are the same positive value W. Conversely (8) has
A=h(N-1)W=h(T-W), so it attains equality.

To prove necessity, if any adjacent weights are unequal, (2) is
strict above their minimum on a positive-length open interval.
Therefore equality forces all adjacent weights, hence all weights,
to be the same W>0. Inside [u_0,u_(N-1)] the actual root-volume is
at least W^(1/s), by (2). It is continuous on the interior of its
projection, by concavity. Equality of the integral forces its
volume to equal W everywhere between these two endpoints.

There can be no nonempty fiber outside this base interval: its
convex hull with a full positive-volume endpoint fiber would add
a positive amount of (s+1)-volume outside the interval. Thus the
real projection is exactly [u_0,u_(N-1)]. Let K_0,K_1 be its two
endpoint fibers. They have equal positive volume W. Their midpoint
Minkowski average is contained in the midpoint fiber, also of
volume W. Equality in Brunn--Minkowski makes K_0 and K_1 translates.
At every intermediate u, the corresponding Minkowski interpolation
is a translate of K_0, is contained in Q_u, and has the same volume
as Q_u. Containment of full-dimensional compact convex bodies of
equal volume is equality. This proves (8), including s=1.

If T>0 and N=1, the right side of (1) is zero. Equality holds
exactly when Q consists of that single sampled s-dimensional fiber:
any additional base point and the positive sampled fiber would
span a cone of positive (s+1)-volume. If T=0 (including no sampled
bases), equality in (1) is simply A=0. These cases do not assert
full dimension for Q.

## 4. A dimension-free mass correction for one fine coordinate

Let Q_z be finitely many compact convex sets in R times R^s with
the same grid a+hZ. They may be actual coarse fibers of a larger
convex body. Let J>=1 be the number of coarse levels with any
nonempty fine sample, let T be their total sampled s-volume, and
let M be the sum of their (s+1)-volumes. Additional coarse levels
without fine samples may be included in M. Assume T>0. On each
sampled level choose its largest sampled volume W_z. Formula (1)
and summation give

    sum_z W_z >= T-M/h.                                 (9)

Thus some ACTUAL fine fiber has volume at least

    W_global >= (T-M/h)_+/J.                            (10)

Take its ordinary continuous centroid. This point belongs to the
original mixed source. Every containing original ambient closed
halfspace restricts to a containing halfspace or to the whole
s-dimensional fine fiber, so ordinary Grunbaum supplies at least
Gamma_s W_global unnormalized mass from that fiber alone. Hence

    max depth_original
       >= [Gamma_s/J] (1-M/(hT))_+.                     (11)

The common factor h in covolume-weighted fine measure cancels in
this normalized formula. In a convex source with k coarse integer
coordinates and this one fine integer coordinate, the explicit
conditions

    J<=2^k,       M/(hT)<=1/2                            (12)

therefore imply the exact target Gamma_s/2^(k+1), for every s>=1,
using ONLY the ordinary continuous theorem. This improves the
volume-ratio condition 1/[2(s+1)] obtained from the full-rank
factorial estimate. It does not require sampled affine rank zero:
the peak bound applies uniformly to both one-sample and multi-sample
coarse levels. The condition J<=2^k remains an explicit restriction.

The endpoint budget in (12) has an exact calibration. Let the coarse
projection be the binary k-cube, the fine real base interval [0,h],
and every continuous fiber the same s-simplex K. There are 2^(k+1)
actual fine fibers, all at exposed base vertices. Here J=2^k and
M/(hT)=1/2. An ambient cap can isolate a fiber and realize any of
its continuous cap cuts. The maximal depth is exactly
Gamma_s/2^(k+1), attained at a fiber centroid. Thus (11) and (12)
are sharp on this family.

## 5. Applying the inequality to an oblique cap

For every ambient halfspace H, each Q_z intersect H is again
compact convex in the fine (u,x)-coordinates. Apply (1) with its
OWN nonempty sampled support and write W_z(H) for its largest
sampled cap volume, or zero if it has none. Then

    h sum_z W_z(H) >= h T(H)-M(H).                       (13)

This is a simultaneous statement for all cap directions, not an
assumption that the cap and complement share a maximizing fiber.
Write H={ell>=0}. Its OPEN complement also satisfies (13): apply
the compact-convex result to Q_z intersect {ell<=-epsilon} and let
epsilon decrease to zero. Monotone convergence handles the coarse
volumes and every sampled fiber volume. The original sampled base
set is finite, so their maxima also converge to the corresponding
open-complement maximum. Since a closed cap and its open complement
partition both measures exactly, this gives, for EVERY orientation,

    h sum_z[W_z(H)+W_z(H^c_open)] >= hT-M.               (14)

In particular purely base cuts and their full sampled boundary
fibers are covered with no double counting. If the continuous
x-normal is nonzero, every sampled boundary has zero s-volume;
then H^c_open can equivalently be replaced in (14) by the opposite
CLOSED halfspace with the same boundary.

The direct center bound (11) avoids these possible changes of
maximizing fiber and already holds for EVERY original containing
halfspace. No stronger common-peak or multi-level allocation claim
is inferred from (13)--(14).
